theme: Comfort in suffering; the new covenant ministry
readingInstruction: Read 2 Corinthians 1:1-3:18. Paul writes his most personal letter. Notice the comfort in suffering in chapter 1, the aroma of Christ in chapter 2, and the new covenant ministry in chapter 3.
settingTheScene: After writing 1 Corinthians, Paul’s relationship with the church became strained. He made a painful visit, wrote a severe letter (now lost), and waited anxiously for news from Titus. When Titus brought good news in Macedonia, Paul wrote 2 Corinthians, a letter full of emotion. It defends his ministry against critics who called him weak and unimpressive, and it reveals the heart of a pastor who suffers for his people. Chapters 1 to 3 introduce the main themes: comfort through affliction and the glory of the new covenant.
observation: “The Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (1:3).
“Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead” (1:9).
“For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (1:20).
“Who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee” (1:22).
“You show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (3:3).
“Who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (3:6).
“Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (3:17).
“Beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (3:18).
interpretation:
Paul opens with a blessing: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” Comfort is not a private possession. We receive in order to give. Suffering abounds for Christ, but through Christ comfort abounds too. He describes a recent affliction in Asia that was so severe that they despaired of life. “Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.” Suffering teaches dependence.

He explains why he did not come to Corinth as planned: he was sparing them. His “Yes” is not “Yes and No.” Then a beautiful statement on the faithfulness of God: “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.” Christ is the fulfillment of every promise. It is God who establishes us with you in Christ, anointed us, “put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.” The Spirit is the down payment on our inheritance.

Chapter 2 refers to the painful letter written “out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears.” When someone had caused grief, the church disciplined him. Now Paul says it is time to forgive and comfort him, “so that he may not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” Forgiveness protects against Satan’s schemes. Then a picture of triumph: “But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through him spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.” The image is of a Roman victory parade, with incense burning. For some it is the aroma of life; for others, death. “Who is sufficient for these things?” Not Paul, but God.

In chapter 3, Paul defends his credentials. “You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts… a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.” This echoes Ezekiel 36 and Jeremiah 31. Our competence is from God, “who has made us competent to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” The old covenant, engraved in letters on stone, came with glory, but it was a ministry of death and condemnation, fading. The new covenant ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness has far greater glory, and it remains. This is a key text for progressive covenantalism: the old covenant was glorious, but it was temporary, and the new covenant exceeds it in glory. Moses put a veil over his face so the Israelites would not gaze at the fading glory. A veil lies over hearts when the old covenant is read, “because only through Christ is it taken away.”

The chapter ends with freedom and transformation. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.” We become what we behold. By looking at Christ in Scripture, we are changed.
connection: Exodus 34:29-35 tells of Moses’ veil. Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Ezekiel 36:26-27 promise the new covenant. Romans 8:1-4 and 15:4 are related. Ephesians 1:13-14 speaks of the seal and guarantee. Isaiah 51:12 speaks of comfort. Philippians 3:3-11 compares old and new. Hebrews 8 to 10 explain the superiority of the new covenant. Colossians 1:15 calls Christ the image of God. Romans 12:2 speaks of transformation.
application:
Think of a suffering you have been through. Whom can you now comfort with the comfort you received?

Spend ten minutes looking at Christ in a Gospel passage and ask the Spirit to transform you.

Thank God that all his promises are Yes in Christ. Say “Amen” to a specific promise.
prayerPrompts: Thank the Father of mercies for comforting you.
Ask him to help you comfort someone else with the comfort you received.
Thank him for the ministry of the new covenant.
